thread.title: Is This the Week That the Market Takes Trade Fears Seriously?

author: Martin Tillier
title: Is This the Week That the Market Takes Trade Fears Seriously?
text:
Shutterstock photo If you have been awake and paying attention at any point in the last year or so it should come as no surprise that trade and tariffs will be the main subjects of interest this week for market watchers.
It is, after all, that way just about every week.
There is a danger that the constant drip, drip of trade-related stories and the lack of a significant reaction in the market will blind investors as to how impactful this ongoing story could be, and people could be caught flat-footed when the market starts to perceive a serious threat. That could well be this week.
We have become so used to hearing about another round of import taxes here and more retaliation there that we have lost sight of the cumulative effect, so a steady market this morning as traders brace for tariffs on another $200 billion of imported Chinese goods is not really that surprising. If anything, traders are likely to heave a sigh of relief as stories are leaking that this round of punitive taxes on China will be “only” ten percent rather than the twenty-five percent many had feared. “Not as bad as it could have been” however, is rarely a good reason for optimism in trading.
Still, in this case, the piecemeal way these tariffs have been enacted is what gives the bulls hope. They maintain it is an indicator of the strategic nature of the policy and a reminder that President Trump sees tariffs as negotiating tools, and therefore short term by definition. Once better deals have been negotiated, they maintain, these punitive measures will be abandoned, and America will be trading from a better position going forward.
There is also another, more cynical way of looking at it, but that leads to the same result. It could be that the whole thing is political theater. The purpose of the frequent announcements of new rounds of tariffs is to reassure Trump supporters that their man is on top of things and sticking it to foreigners as the mid-term elections approach.
Again, in this scenario any potential negative economic consequences will be minimized, or even avoided all together, as the tariffs will be abandoned when the political goal is achieved.
The problem with that reasoning is that things only play out that way if one side or another gives in, and so far, there is no reason for either the Trump administration nor the Chinese government to cave. Both can point to data and say that they are winning the war.
From Trump’s perspective, continued strong growth both in terms of GDP and employment numbers indicates that the wailing and gnashing of teeth by economists when the first tariffs were enacted was a typical overreaction by political opponents in a severely polarized environment.
China and others affected by tariffs will point to the latest available trade data. That showed that the U.S. trade deficit hit another record high in July with both China and the E.U.
In both cases, the protagonists can claim with some justification that they are winning. Is it possible that both are correct? No, it isn’t.
Economic changes take a long time to filter through into data that is by nature historical, and the tendency of businesses to look forward can often lead to confusing short-term distortions as the ill-effects of policy loom. Stockpiling by U.S. importers convinced that their industry will be the next hit, and even savvy consumers bringing purchases forward in anticipation of higher prices, could go a long way towards explaining the higher trade deficit and strong growth.
The Trump administration’s biggest success so far has been in the way that the attitude of corporate America has changed. Whether you like it and believe it to be true or not, many business owners and management felt that they were disadvantaged under President Obama. Regulations and restrictions on their businesses were seemingly coming every day, and confidence in the future was still low despite the recovery. Tax cuts and deregulation have changed that, but over the last couple of days there are some signs that the persistence of the trade wars could be affecting that confidence.
Those worst affected have started to fight back, at least in the realm of P.R.
Until recently most corporations, even those directly impacted by tariffs, have kept quiet, presumably afraid of a nasty tweet from the White House. Companies as diverse as Nike ( NKE ), Apple ( AAPL ) and Harley Davidson ( HOG ) that received that treatment, however, have seen business little affected, and in some cases even boosted by the attendant publicity. That will give others the courage to speak out, and a growing tide of discontent from large companies will serve to quickly dispel the prevalent buoyant mood.
So, if this week brings the expected and predictable tax hikes on a couple of hundred billion dollars-worth of imports and the equally predictable retaliation/escalation, it may not be greeted with the shrug of the shoulders that we have come to expect. As the realization grows that no party in these disputes feels the need to back down and as normally reliably Republican corporate leaders voice concern that could erode confidence, this could be the week that the market starts to take trade seriously.
